content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper aims to address the multi-domain long-tailed recognition problem.         
(1) An augmentation strategy is proposed for this goal:     
I. For each time, uniformly sample an image across all classes and uniformly sample an image across all domains.     
II. Each image representation is disentangled by class-relevant features and domain-relevant features.     
III. Combining the semantic representation of one with the domain-related nuisance factors of the other to form the augmented representation.    

(2) Experiments are conducted on several long-tailed datasets with subpopulation shift and domain shift. Clear improvements are observed.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:    
(1) The paper writes clear and is easy to follow.    
(2) The method is simple and elegant.    
(3) Experiments on different benchmarks show good improvements over baselines.    
(4) Sound ablations are conducted.  

Weakness:     
(1) Some long-tailed methods are selected as baselines, like CRT, and MiSLAS. However, state-of-the-art long-tailed methods can be transferred to this multi-domain long-tailed recognition task, like PaCo [1], and RIDE [2].    

(2) Would the representation augmentation module be removed at inference?    

(3)  Regular augmentations like RandAug can also improve performance. Can the proposed TALLY work with them?

(4) Can the proposed TALLY  work with long-tailed methods like PaCo [1], and RIDE[2]?


[1] Parametric Contrastive Learning. ICCV 2021.
[2] Long-tailed Recognition by Routing Diverse Distribution-Aware Experts. ICLR 2021.

**A1**: We conducted additional experiments to show the performance of PaCo and RIDE under the multi-domain long-tailed recognition setting. The ablation study demonstrated that the proposed approach works better on small-size classes and can learn more domain-invariant features.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ijLa (1/3)
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable feedback to help us improve our paper. We have revised our paper according to your comments. We respond to your questions below and would appreciate it if you could let us know whether your concerns are addressed by our response.

**Q1**: The difference between the selective balanced sampling strategy and balanced sampling is unclear. I read Section 3.2 and “Analysis of sampling strategies” but still confusing. Figure 3 does not do a good job on explain the difference either. What is the difference between y, d ~ Uniform(C, D) vs y~ Uniform(C) and d ~Uniform(D)? Can you explain more about the transition probabilities in Figure 3?

**A1**: In Figure 3, there are three domain-class groups: (Fan, Clipart), (Fan, Art), (Computer, Clipart) and the number of examples for each group is 1, 13, 83, respectively. We specifically focus on augmenting examples from the minority group (i.e., (Computer, Clipart) group). In this case, the samples $(x_i, y_i, d_i)$ and $(x_j, y_j, d_j)$ need to contain class semantic information (i.e., Fan) and domain information (i.e., Clipart) in the representation augmentation module, respectively.

The balanced sampling under the multi-domain long-tailed classification problem is to up-sample examples from minority domain-class groups. Concretely, the label $y_i$ and domain $d_i$ for each example $(x_i, y_i, d_i)$ are jointly sampled from $\mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D})$. If we employ original balanced sampling in the representation augmentation module of TALLY, then $(y_i, d_i)\sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D})$, $(y_j, d_j)\sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{C}, \mathcal{D})$. To augment the (Fan, Clipart) group, the class semantic information from $(x_i, y_i, d_i)$ has a 1/2 probability to be obtained from the original (**Fan**, Clipart) group, and a 1/2 probability to be obtained from the (**Fan**, Art) group. Similarly, the domain information has a 1/2 probability to be obtained from the original (Fan, **Clipart**) group, and a 1/2 probability to be obtained from the (Computer, **Clipart**) group. Thus, examples from the minority group (i.e., Fan, Clipart) will be repeatedly sampled during the augmentation process and this is what we do not expect.

Instead, for selective balanced sampling, the label $y_i$ of example $i$ is uniformly sampled from all classes (i.e., $y_i\sim \mathrm{Uniform}(\mathcal{C})$), and the domain $d_j$ or example $j$ is uniformly sampled from all domains (i.e., $d_i\sim \mathrm(\mathcal{D})$). Thus, to augment the (Fan, Clipart) group, the class semantic information from example $(x_i, y_i, d_i)$ has a 1/14 probability to be obtained from the original (**Fan**, Clipart) group and a 13/14 probability to be obtained from the (**Fan**, Art) group because we do not consider domain information in sampling example $(x_i, y_i, d_i)$. Similarly, for selective balanced sampling, the domain information has a 1/84 probability to be obtained from the original (Fan, **Clipart**) group, and a 83/84 probability to be obtained from the (Computer, **Clipart**) group. 

To sum up, using selective balanced sampling can provide more diverse and effective knowledge transfer. We added these detailed explanations in Appendix A.1 of the revised paper.

---

**Q2**: For the evaluation protocol, it is unclear what exactly is held-out? It seems in the long-tailed learning setting, all the classes and domains (except for one) are seen. It is very important to make sure there is no information leakage from training to test sets, and that the comparisons are fair.

**A2**: We detail our ways to split the dataset below and edit the text in Appendix D.2 (synthetic datasets), and E.2 (real-world datasets) of the revised paper.  All baselines use the same evaluation protocol and no additional information is provided for TALLY. Thus, the comparison between TALLY and all baselines is fair.

- **Subpopulation shift**: In subpopulation shift, the training distribution for each domain is a long-tailed distribution and the test is domain-class balanced distribution, i.e., the number of examples in each domain-class pair is the same. 
- **Domain shift in synthetic data**: In terms of domain shifts in synthetic datasets, following [Peng et al. ICCV 2019; Shi et al. ICLR 2022], we hold out one domain as the testing domain and use the rest domains as training. 
- **Domain shift in real-world data**: In terms of domain shifts in real-world data, we follow [Koh et al. ICML 2021] and use the same split as they did for iWildCam, where a bunch of locations is selected for testing and the rest ones are used for training. For TerraInc, we adopt the same strategy to split training and test domains since TerraInc also focuses on wildlife recognition and the data distribution is similar to iWildCam.

content.title: Response to Reviewer ijLa (2/3)
content.comment:
**Q3**: The paper considered a wide range of baselines, including both domain adaptation and domain generalization methods. It would be helpful to explain the underlying assumptions of different methods, such as whether labels or data from the target domain is needed. 

**A3**: In both settings with subpopulation shift and domain shift, no labels or any kind of data from the target domain are needed for all baselines. All baselines adopt the same evaluation protocol, i.e., no additional information is used for TALLY. We have clarified it in Appendix D.2 and E.2 in the revised paper.

---

**Q4**: Is equation (4) possible for a new unseen domain?

**A4**: The representation augmentation module is only used during the training stage. Thus, equation (4) is only applied to training domains. We clarified it and put the pseudocode of the testing stage in Algorithm 2 of Appendix A.2 in the revised paper.

---

**Q5**: How does the presented work compare to a simpler approach: train on imbalanced and fine-tune on balanced datasets? For example, domain-specific transfer learning?

**A5**: We conducted an additional experiment to compare TALLY with the simpler approach that you mentioned here. Here, we adopted three variants of balanced datasets for fine-tuning: (i) class-balanced dataset, where the number of examples is the same across different classes; (ii) domain-balanced dataset, where the number of examples is the same across different domains; (iii) domain-class balanced dataset, where the number of examples is the same across each domain-class group. We report the results in Table R1.

**Table R1**: Performance comparison between TALLY and balanced finetuning on synthetic data with subpopulation shifts. FT means fine-tuning.

|                          |  Subpopulation shift  |                       |      Domain shift     |                     |
|--------------------------|:---------------------:|:---------------------:|:---------------------:|:-------------------:|
| Dataset                  |     OfficeHome-LT     |      DomainNet-LT     |        TerraInc       |       iWildCam      |
| Metric                   |     Balanced Acc.     |     Balanced Acc.     |        Macro F1       |       Macro F1      |
| Class-balanced FT        |   63.41 $\pm$ 0.32%  |   47.23 $\pm$ 0.83%  |   44.36 $\pm$ 0.45%  |   32.5 $\pm$ 0.3%   |
| Domain-balanced FT       |   61.19 $\pm$ 0.79%  |   44.32 $\pm$ 0.28%  |   43.92 $\pm$ 0.77%  |   32.9 $\pm$ 0.8%   |
| Domain-class-balanced FT |   62.84 $\pm$ 0.28%  |   47.07 $\pm$ 0.41%  |   44.21 $\pm$ 0.31%  |   32.1 $\pm$ 0.5%   |
| **TALLY**                | **67.00 $\pm$ 0.47%** | **50.15 $\pm$ 0.46%** | **46.23 $\pm$ 0.56%** | **34.4 $\pm$ 0.4%** |



According to the results, we observe that TALLY still outperforms all variants of balanced finetuning, indicating its effectiveness in addressing the multi-domain long-tailed learning problem by augmenting disentangled representations. Full results with more evaluation metrics and discussions are added in Appendix F.1.

---

**Q6**: The concept of subpopulation shift is confusing. Conventionally, it refers to the setting that the supclass remains the same but the subclasses comprising each supclass are different across domains. It seems here it means training domains are imbalanced but the classes in the test domain are balanced. This seems to be a convention in long-tailed learning, although may not be realistic. It is more related to the long-tailed setting, rather than the subpopulation shift in domain adaptation. Would it be better to report performance vs class size such as in Figure 4?

**A6**: We follow [Koh et al. ICML 2021] to define subpopulation shift. As we mentioned in Section 2, in this definition, both training and test distributions can be formulated as a mixture distribution over domain space $\mathcal{D}$, i.e., $P^{tr}=\sum_{d=1}^D \eta_d^{tr} P^{tr}_d$,

$P^{ts}=\sum_{d=1}^D \eta_d^{ts} P^{ts}_d$. In subpopulation shift, all test domains are seen at the training stage, but the proportions of the domains can change, i.e., $\eta_d^{tr}\neq \eta_d^{ts}$ for each $d\in \mathcal{D}$. Based on this definition, in subpopulation shift, we leverage domain-class balanced accuracy as the primary metric to evaluate the performance and also conduct some analysis to show the performance v.s. Class size in Figure 4.

---

**Q7**: What does TALLY stand for?

**A7**: TALLY represents mul**T**i-dom**A**in **L**ong-tailed learning with ba**L**anced representation reassembl**Y**. We have clarified it in the introduction.

content.title: Response to Reviewer nEAQ
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable and constructive comments and feedback. We address your concerns below, and have revised our paper accordingly. We would appreciate it if you could let us know whether your concerns are addressed by our response.

**Q1**: Representation disentangle and date augmentation are the common approaches for long-tailed recognition, and no novel approach is proposed for the specific issue of multi-domain long-tailed recognition.

**A1**: Prior works, including [Zhong et al. CVPR 2021], [Zhou et al. ICLR 2022], have noted the effectiveness of data augmentation in long-tailed recognition. As stated in the related work section, all of these methods focus on the single-domain long-tailed recognition problem, while TALLY targets the multi-domain long-tailed recognition problem, while multi-domain long-tailed recognition brings a unique challenge: the machine learning model is supposed to handle the class imbalance issue and learn class-invariant representation simultaneously. To address this problem, TALLY empowers balanced augmentation over classes and domains to solve the class imbalance issue. Meanwhile, TALLY leverages prototypes to cancel out domain-related information and achieves invariant representations. We believe that TALLY is a novel approach that is specifically designed for multi-domain long-tailed recognition.

---

**Q2**: why the representation of each examples can be decoupled into semantic information and nuisances, and the domain information is contained in nuisances?

**A2**: The domain information is contained in nuisances. Following [Zhou et al. ICLR 2022], nuisance is defined as "class-agnostic" transformations that apply similarly to all classes, such as image style and background changes in image classification. We edited the text in the first paragraph of Section 3 to clarify this naming.

In addition, decoupling representations to class-related semantic information and class-agnostic domain information has already been adopted in many problems, such as domain adaptation [Peng et al. ICML 2019] and generative modeling [Gabbay et al. ICLR 2020]. 

---

**Q3**: The construction of prototype is too simple to ineffective. I think the updating of prototypes is needed.

**A3**: We indeed updated the prototype in every iteration (see Line 13 - 16 in Algorithm 1). Additionally, we already empirically showed the effectiveness of the prototype with an ablation study in the paragraph “How do prototypes benefit invariant learning” of Section 4.4.

In terms of the complexity of prototype construction, we have investigated more complicated prototype construction strategies. Specifically, we leveraged DeepSets transformation discussed in [Ye et al. CVPR 2020] to model the correlations between different prototypes. We report the results in Table R1. Here, using DeepSets to advance prototypes is denoted as Advanced Prototype.

**Table R1**: Comparison with different prototype construction strategies.

|                          |  Subpopulation shift  |                       |      Domain shift     |                     |
|--------------------------|:---------------------:|:---------------------:|:---------------------:|:-------------------:|
| Dataset                  |     OfficeHome-LT     |      DomainNet-LT     |        TerraInc       |       iWildCam      |
| Metric                   |     Balanced Acc.     |     Balanced Acc.     |        Macro F1       |       Macro F1      |
| Advanced Prototype |   65.12 $\pm$ 0.21%   |   49.05 $\pm$ 0.70%   |   44.12 $\pm$ 0.44%   |   32.7$\pm$ 0.3%    |
| **TALLY**          | **67.00 $\pm$ 0.47%** | **50.15 $\pm$ 0.46%** | **46.23 $\pm$ 0.56%** | **34.4 $\pm$ 0.4%** |


According to the results in Table R1, we observe that the vanilla prototype construction strategy shows better performance compared to other strategies. The potential reason is that it might be hard to train a well-performed transformation that can accurately capture the correlations behind prototypes. We thus use the vanilla prototype construction method.

---

**References**:

[Zhong et al. CVPR 2021] Zhong, Zhisheng, Jiequan Cui, Shu Liu, and Jiaya Jia. "Improving calibration for long-tailed recognition." CVPR 2021.

[Zhou et al. ICLR 2022] Zhou, Allan, Fahim Tajwar, Alexander Robey, Tom Knowles, George J. Pappas, Hamed Hassani, and Chelsea Finn. "Do Deep Networks Transfer Invariances Across Classes?." ICLR 2022.

[Peng et al. ICML 2019] Peng, Xingchao, Zijun Huang, Ximeng Sun, and Kate Saenko. "Domain agnostic learning with disentangled representations." ICLR 2019.

[Gabbay et al. ICLR 2020] Gabbay, Aviv, and Yedid Hoshen. "Demystifying Inter-Class Disentanglement." ICLR 2020.

[Ye et al. CVPR 2020] Ye, Han-Jia, Hexiang Hu, De-Chuan Zhan, and Fei Sha. "Few-shot learning via embedding adaptation with set-to-set functions." CVPR 2020.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper focuses on multi-domain long-tail classification, where each domain has its own long-tailed distribution. To solve this problem, the authors propose a novel balanced augment method TALLY, which separates and reassembles class-relevant semantic information and domain-associated nuisance information. Specifically, first, the representation of each instance is divided into semantic representation and nuisances. Then the semantic information and domain-associated factors are separately enhanced using argument techniques to improve stability and reduce noise. Finally, the semantic information and nuisances are reassembled to generate new instances for training. Several experiments on four synthetic multi-domain long-tailed datasets and two real-world datasets indicate that the proposed methods improve the overall performance for subpopulation shift and domain shift compared to two types of baselines.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
This paper focuses on a less-studied problem and defines the problem formally. With an example on the real-world dataset and some discussion, the authors illustrate why it is not trivial to explore the problem. Unlike single-domain long-tail classification, the authors figure out that multi-domains exist with their own long-tail distributions, and previous approaches may exacerbate class imbalance in this scenario.
For the implementation details of the proposed method, the authors give good motivation. For example, in proposing selective balanced sampling, the authors illustrate by figure the drawbacks of balanced sampling from all domain-class groups and how selective balanced sampling solves this problem.
The proposed approach is relatively novel. Although some of the techniques are derived from existing work, such as the representation disentanglement and reassembly section, the authors provide some new technical insights.
The experimental results broadly validate the authors' claim that TALLY is more effective than the existing single-domain imbalanced classification and domain-invariant learning methods under subpopulation shift and domain shift tasks. In addition, sufficient experiments are carried out to demonstrate the importance of each component in TALLY.
However, my main concerns are some details in the model and experimental part of this paper. Here are the detailed comments:
[Presentation] The paper's writing and statements are easy to follow. However, I have some minor suggestions. (1) Since one of the main contributions of the paper is to formalize the multi-domain long-tailed learning problem, clearer notation should be given to help future works better understand the problem and better use these notations. For example, the meanings of some symbols are explained but remain complex, considering the different superscripts and subscripts. (2) Also, some definitions should be better given in more obvious places, such as class-agnostic statistics u_d^{(0)} and v_d^{(0)}.
Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, but some theoretical analysis can be given to shed light on the algorithm designs of TALLY and inspire future work.
[Experiments] On domain generalization benchmarks, overall performance is used to measure the performance of subpopulation shift and domain shift; on naturally imbalanced multi-domain data, macro F1 score and average accuracy are used. However, I am not sure of the reason for using these measures. Considering that we are exploring the multi-domain long-tailed problem, should some evaluation metrics that measure tail performance be considered?
[Reproducibility] Although the critical parts of the method are carefully clarified with the pseudo algorithm, the code of this paper is not given, which limits the reproducibility of this paper.

content.title: Response to Reviewer yuqM
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our paper and for your valuable feedback. We have simplified our notations and revised our paper based on your feedback. We detail our response below and please kindly let us know if our response addresses your concerns.

**Q1**: the meanings of some symbols are explained but remain complex, considering the different superscripts and subscripts

**A1**: Thanks for pointing it out. We made the following two changes to simplify our notations:

-  We removed the superscript “tr” in denoting the number of examples for each training class or domain in Sections 2 and 3 (Eqn. (5) and (7)), i.e., $n_c^{tr}$ and $n_d^{tr}$ are modified as $n_c$ and $n_d$, respectively. 

- We removed the subscript $i$ in both Eqn. (6) and (8) since both equations are generic in constructing prototypes.

---

**Q2**: some definitions should be better given in more obvious places, such as class-agnostic statistics u_d^{(0)} and v_d^{(0)}

**A2**: Thanks for pointing it out. We added the definition of these statistics below Equation 8 (“In practice, we update … and $v_d^{(t)}$, respectively”).

---

**Q3**: Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method, but some theoretical analysis can be given to shed light on the algorithm designs of TALLY and inspire future work.

**A3**: Thanks for the great suggestion. We plan to conduct theoretical studies to better understand the empirical phenomena of TALLY and other methods in the future. 

---

**Q4**: Using macro F1 score and average accuracy.

**A4**: We follow [Koh et al. ICML 2021] and report Marco F1 and average accuracy on iWildCam. It is worthwhile to point out that Macro F1 emphasized the performance of rare/minority classes. The TerraInc dataset has very similar properties to iWildCam and thus we also use these two metrics to evaluate the performance. In synthetic data, to emphasize the performance on minority classes and domains, we use domain-class balanced accuracy as the evaluation metric. We detailed the discussion of evaluation metrics in Appendix B.2 of the revised paper.

---

**Q5**: Considering that we are exploring the multi-domain long-tailed problem, should some evaluation metrics that measure tail performance be considered?

**A5**: We use domain-class balanced accuracy and Macro F1 to measure the performance on synthetic datasets and real-world datasets, respectively. Both metrics emphasize the performance of tail classes. Additionally, we already evaluated the results w.r.t. class size in Figure 4 in our paper. According to the results, we observe that TALLY's performance improvements arise from larger improvements on smaller classes rather than performance improvements across the board, indicating its effectiveness to handle class-imbalanced problems.

---

**Q6**: Reproducibility and code releasing

**A6**: Thanks for pointing it out. We released the code via an official comment. Please kindly let us know if you have any additional suggestions about reproducibility.

content.title: Paper Decision
content.metareview:_summary,_strengths_and_weakn:
Summary:
This paper proposes a data-augmentation method TALLY for multi-domain long-tailed learning. TALLY provides balanced augmentation by disentangling and resembling class-relevant semantic information and domain-associated nuisance information in the latent domain. The experimental results on synthesis and real-world data show its effectiveness.

Strengths:
- The paper has addressed an important and less studied problem in machine learning -- multi-domain long-tailed learning.
- The experiments are extensive and valid.
- The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

Weaknesses:
- It has limited novelty because the proposed method is a combination of existing techniques.
- There are missing details on why the representation of each examples can be decoupled into semantic information and nuisances.
content.justification_for_why_not_higher_score: This is a borderline paper. Reviewers acknowledge that this investigation is worthwhile. However, there are shared concerns on the limited novelty, missing details on why the representation of each examples can be decoupled into semantic information and nuisances, the reproducibility and the evaluation of the proposed algorithm. The authors address some of these, providing code and revised paper, but these were not enough to sway reviewers. I think this paper is not ready for publication at the current stage due to limited novelty.
content.summary_of_AC-reviewer_meeting:
During the virtual meeting, all reviewers agreed that the paper has addressed an important and less studied problem in machine learning -- multi-domain long-tailed learning, the paper is well written, and the experiments are sound. Most reviewers have concern on the limited novelty of the proposed method.

Reviewer yuqM mentioned that the authors' feedback has answered his doubt about the reproducibility and evaluation of the proposed algorithm, therefore he increased score from 3 to 5. He still has concern on the limited novelty because the proposed method is a combination of existing techniques.

Reviewer nEAQ didn't attend the meeting.

Reviewer ijLa still thinks that the paper is a borderline paper. There is no strong reason to either reject or accept it.

Reviewer WENZ is more positive about the paper. He thinks that the proposed method is interesting and is a new combination that's different from previous work.

I weight the concern on the limited novelty more for the final decision.
